weeks.title: Two Planets, Two Operating Systems
weeks.reading: Chapter 1 · Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus
ideas: The core metaphor: partners aren't wrong, they're foreign — conflict comes from expecting the other person to think like you.
questions: Before reading, what did you expect this book to say? What has surprised you so far — in either direction?
Gray's premise is that most relationship pain comes from misreading difference as rejection. Think of a recent conflict (romantic, family, or friend): does that lens change how you see it?
weeks.tryIt: Start small: notice one moment this week when you (or someone else) read a difference as rejection. Bring it Monday.

weeks.title: Two Planets, Two Operating Systems
weeks.reading: Chapters 2–3 · Mr. Fix-It and the Home-Improvement Committee · Men Go to Their Caves and Women Talk
ideas: Mr. Fix-It: men tend to offer solutions when a woman wants to feel heard; the Home-Improvement Committee: women offer unsolicited advice that men hear as criticism.
The cave vs. talking it out: under stress, one style withdraws to process alone; the other processes by talking.
questions: Are you more of a Fix-It or a Home-Improvement Committee person? Who in your life gets the brunt of it?
When you're stressed, do you go to a cave or do you need to talk? What happens when you're close to someone with the opposite style?
Gray assigns these styles by gender. Where does that match your experience, and where does it break down?
What's one phrase from these chapters you could actually use — e.g., asking “do you want solutions or just to vent?”
weeks.angle: Early dating question: when a text goes unanswered for hours, is your instinct “they've withdrawn to their cave” or “they're losing interest”? Discuss how the cave concept could reduce (or excuse!) anxiety-spiraling over response times.
weeks.tryIt: Once this week, when someone shares a problem with you, resist fixing or advising. Just listen and reflect back. Report to each other how it felt and how they responded.

weeks.title: Motivation and Language Barriers
weeks.reading: Chapters 4–5 · How to Motivate the Opposite Sex · Speaking Different Languages
ideas: Gray's claim: men are motivated when they feel needed and trusted; women when they feel cherished and supported.
Same words, different dictionaries: “I'm fine,” “we never go out,” and “nothing's wrong” can be generalizations or feelings, not literal reports.
Not asking for help — or refusing it — as a fear response: fear of rejection on one side, fear of seeming incompetent on the other.
questions: What actually motivates you to show up more fully for someone — feeling needed, feeling appreciated, feeling safe? Does Gray's gender split fit you?
Recall a time you said something like “you never listen” or “it's fine” and meant something bigger. What were you really asking for?
Gray says people stop asking for what they need to avoid rejection, then quietly resent it. Where do you do this?
How do you tell the difference between decoding someone's language and making excuses for someone who's just not communicating?
If a date or partner handed you a translation guide to you, what would its top three entries be?
weeks.angle: Dating anxiety often lives in the gap between what someone said and what we fear they meant. Discuss: what's your worst-case-translation habit (“they said they're busy → they hate me”), and what would a more charitable, evidence-based translation be?
weeks.tryIt: Each of you writes your own three-entry “translation guide” (what I say → what I mean → what I need) and shares it with the others.

weeks.title: Rubber Bands and Waves
weeks.reading: Chapters 6–7 · Men Are Like Rubber Bands · Women Are Like Waves
ideas: The rubber band: a natural cycle of pulling away to regain autonomy, then springing back — withdrawal isn't necessarily rejection.
The wave: emotional wellbeing rises and crashes in cycles; when the wave hits bottom, old feelings surface and what's needed is support, not fixing.
Chasing someone in their pulling-away phase, or fixing someone at the bottom of their wave, backfires.
questions: Do you recognize the rubber band or the wave in yourself — regardless of which one Gray assigned to your gender?
What's your honest reaction when someone you like pulls away: give space, pursue harder, or preemptively withdraw? Where did that pattern come from?
How could you tell the difference between a healthy rubber-band stretch and someone actually checking out of the relationship? What are the observable signs?
When your own wave crashes, what do you actually want from people close to you? Have you ever told them?
Is there a risk in these metaphors — e.g., using “he's just in his cave / stretching his rubber band” to explain away genuinely bad treatment? Where's the line?
weeks.angle: This is the week for the big dating-anxiety conversation: the panic of the pull-away. Discuss a time each of you spiraled when someone got distant. Knowing what you know now, what would you tell your past self — and what boundary would you still keep?
weeks.tryIt: Next time you feel the urge to double-text, chase, or spiral, pause and name it: “rubber band, wave, or real red flag?” Jot down what happened; compare notes at the next meeting.

weeks.title: Emotional Needs, Arguments, and the Scorecard
weeks.reading: Chapters 8–10 · Discovering Our Different Emotional Needs · How to Avoid Arguments · Scoring Points with the Opposite Sex
ideas: Twelve kinds of love (caring, trust, understanding, acceptance, respect, appreciation, devotion, admiration, validation, approval, reassurance, encouragement) — we tend to give the kind we want to receive.
Most arguments aren't about the topic; they're about tone — feeling blamed, dismissed, or unloved while the “issue” gets debated.
Point-scoring: small consistent gestures count more than grand occasional ones; both partners keep score, just differently.
questions: From Gray's twelve kinds of love, which two do you most need? Which do you most naturally give? Are they the same?
Think of a recurring argument in your life. Using Gray's lens, what was it actually about underneath the topic?
Gray says we hurt most where we most need love. Does your biggest sensitivity point to your biggest need?
Do you agree that small, frequent gestures beat grand ones? What “small thing” has meant the most to you in any relationship?
What's your role in arguments — attack, defend, withdraw, or appease? What would de-escalating look like for you specifically?
How do you ask for reassurance without feeling (or seeming) needy? Is “needy” even a fair word?
weeks.angle: Apply the needs list to dating: in early dating, which of your top needs goes unmet the longest — and does that explain the anxiety? What's a reasonable way to get reassurance in something new and undefined?
weeks.tryIt: Pick one person in your life and deliberately give them five “small points” this week — tiny, specific gestures. Notice what it changes in you, not just in them.

weeks.title: Saying the Hard Things and Keeping Love Alive
weeks.reading: Chapters 11–13 · How to Communicate Difficult Feelings · How to Ask for Support and Get It · Keeping the Magic of Love Alive
ideas: The Love Letter technique: writing through anger → sadness → fear → regret → love before having a hard conversation.
Asking for support: be brief, direct, and specific; expect and tolerate a “no” without punishing; “would you” beats “could you.”
Love comes in seasons; old wounds resurface precisely when we feel safe — that's a feature of intimacy, not a failure.
questions: The Love Letter moves through anger, sadness, fear, regret, and love. Which layer do you usually get stuck at — and which do you skip?
Why is asking directly for what we want so hard? What's the story you tell yourself about people who ask plainly?
Gray says tolerating a ‘no’ gracefully is what earns future yeses. How do you actually handle rejection — small ones and big ones?
“Old feelings resurface when we finally feel safe.” Have you seen this — sabotaging or testing something precisely because it was going well?
Looking back on the whole book: which idea will you keep, which will you throw out, and which do you want to argue with Gray about?
Has this book changed how any of you thinks about your dating anxieties? Name one concrete behavior you'll do differently.
weeks.angle: Close the loop: each of you writes down the one dating-anxiety pattern you most want to change and the tool from this book you'll use on it. Say it out loud — that's the accountability part of book club.
weeks.tryIt: Each of you writes a Love Letter (all five layers) about something unresolved — you don't have to send it. Discuss what the exercise surfaced, not necessarily the contents.

further.title: Attached
further.author: Amir Levine & Rachel Heller
further.why: Attachment styles: a more research-based take on the pursue/withdraw dance.
